english.title: Person in charge of a dog allow it to be dangerously out of control in public place and cause injury
english.standardoffencewording: On **(..SPECIFY DATE..) at **(..SPECIFY TOWNSHIP..), were in charge of a dog, namely **(..SPECIFY THE BREED AND DESCRIPTION OF DOG..), which was dangerously out of control in a public place, namely **(..SPECIFY PLACE AND LOCATION..), and whilst so out of control injured **(..SPECIFY PERSON(S)..)
english.legislation: Contrary to section 3(1) and (4) of the Dangerous Dogs Act 1991.

english.notes:
(i) 'Dangerously out of control' was defined in Rafiq v DPP [1997] 161 JP 412 as meaning - when there are grounds for reasonable apprehension that a dog will injure any person, whether or not it does so, if a dog causes injury without first causing anyone reasonable apprehension that it will do so, the injury itself constitutes grounds for reasonable apprehension of injury.
(ii) "Dangerously out of control" does not apply to dogs being used for lawful purposes by the police or a person in the service of the crown, therefore dogs being used lawfully by the police, prison service, military police, and customs and excise, are exempt.
(iii) 'Public place' means any street, road or other place (whether or not enclosed) to which the public have or are permitted to have access whether for payment or otherwise, including the common parts of a building containing two or more dwellings. A postman (and other similar visitors to a house) has a licence from the householder to go up a garden path to the door for the purpose of delivering letters. The garden path to a private dwelling is not (normally) a public place.
(iv) DEFENCE: in proceedings for this offence against an owner who was not in charge of the dog, it is a defence under section 3(2) to prove that the dog was, at the material time, in the charge of a person whom he reasonably believed to be fit and proper to be in charge of it.
(v) A court may make a destruction order and disqualify the offender from having custody of a dog ( section 4 as amended by the Dangerous Dogs (Amendment) Act 1997).
(vi) A court may make a contingent destruction order, see section 4A.
(vii) See also offence wording: H4253.

This offence is obsolete from 13th May 2014. For offences committed after this date see offence documents H11472 (non fatal injury) or H11474 (fatal injury)
